platforms.title: Bed Rest Isn't the Fix for a Sudden Bad Back
platforms.meta_description: Put your back out? NHS advice is to keep moving, skip long bed rest, use ibuprofen and ice or heat, and call 999 for numbness, leg weakness or bladder changes.
platforms.body_html:
You bend to pick up a laundry basket, something catches low in your back, and suddenly getting off the floor feels like a project. The instinct is to lie flat for a few days and wait for it to pass. The NHS advice points the other way. Staying in bed for long periods is on its "don't" list for back pain, and keeping up your normal activities is on the "do" list. That sounds harsh when every movement hurts, so it helps to understand what is actually going on.

Bed Rest Isn't the Fix for a Sudden Bad Back

According to the NHS page on back pain, lower back pain is very common and usually improves within a few weeks, although it can last longer or come back. A common cause is an injury such as a pulled muscle, which the NHS calls a strain. Sometimes a slipped disc or sciatica, where a nerve is trapped, is behind it. Very rarely, back pain is a sign of something serious such as a broken bone, an infection or cancer. In most sudden cases, though, it is not obvious what caused it, and it gets better on its own.

The muscles around a strained area tend to tighten up to guard it. That guarding is what makes your back feel locked. Lying still for days does not unlock it; the muscles stiffen further and getting up becomes harder each time. This is why NHS self-care advice starts with movement: stay active and try to continue with your daily activities, even if you have to do them more slowly. Gentle activity keeps the joints moving and the muscles working, which is what recovery needs.

The NHS also lists activities such as walking, swimming, yoga and pilates as things that may help ease back pain. You do not need a full routine on day one. A few slow laps of the house, a short walk to the corner shop, or standing up every so often while you work all count.

Skip the Sofa Marathon: Here's What Helps

Painkillers are there to make moving possible, not to replace it. The NHS suggests anti-inflammatory medicine such as ibuprofen, noting that it may not be suitable for everyone. Paracetamol on its own is not recommended for back pain, although it may be used alongside another painkiller. If you are unsure which painkiller is suitable for you, the NHS says to check with a pharmacist or GP before you start.

Ice and heat each have a job. The NHS says an ice pack, or a bag of frozen peas, wrapped in a tea towel can reduce pain and swelling, while a heat pack or hot water bottle wrapped in a tea towel can relieve stiffness or muscle spasms. Keep a layer of fabric between the pack and your skin either way. Many people find heat more comfortable once the first sharp phase has passed, but there is no prize for choosing correctly; use whichever lets you move more.

Back exercises and stretches can also help, and the NHS has a physiotherapist-led stretching video and a pilates workout for back pain. Stop if your pain gets worse and ask a GP for advice. In many areas you can now refer yourself to NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) services for physiotherapy without seeing a GP first, which is worth knowing if things are slow to settle.

If You Change One Thing Today

Swap one long rest on the sofa for several short spells on your feet. That single change follows the core NHS message: movement helps, long bed rest does not. Then watch the trend. The NHS says to see a GP if the pain does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks, if it is stopping you doing your day-to-day activities, if it does not improve after resting or is worse at night, or if it is worse when sneezing, coughing or pooing. Unexplained weight loss, a lump or a change in the shape of your back are also reasons to book in.

When a Bad Back Is an Emergency

A small number of symptoms change the advice completely, because they can mean the nerves at the bottom of the spine are being squeezed, a condition called cauda equina syndrome. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if you have back pain and any of these:

  • pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
  • loss of feeling around your genitals or anus
  • changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself
  • changes in sexual sensation or function
  • chest pain, or pain that started after a serious accident such as a car crash

Do not drive yourself to A&E; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance, and bring your medicines. For less dramatic warning signs, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if you feel hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell, or if severe pain starts suddenly or is getting worse quickly.

So here is a question to ask yourself tonight: have you been up and moving at least a little every few hours today, and have you checked that none of the 999 signs apply? This article is general information and does not replace advice from your GP or pharmacist.

Sources: NHS, "Back pain" (page last reviewed 5 March 2026).
